## formal
Let the modes on one null generator carry a generator momentum $k$ in the window $I = \{-N, \dots, N - 1\}$ and a channel $\alpha$ in a finite set; each mode $(k, \alpha)$ is a tower plane with $a_{k,\alpha}^{*} = v$, $a_{k,\alpha} = w$ (Theorem \claimref{tower.ladder-pairs-satisfy-car-vectors}), with the adjoint $*$ ($v^{*} = w$). Numbers are read in $\mathrm{span}\{1, J\}$, $J = g_{1}g_{2}$ the kernel bivector, which commutes with every mode, $J^{2} = -1$, $J^{*} = -J$. For a channel matrix $M$ with entries in $\mathrm{span}\{1, J\}$ ($M^{*}$ its conjugate transpose) and $q \ge 0$ let $\rho_{q}(M) = \sum_{k, k+q \in I}\sum_{\alpha,\beta}M_{\alpha\beta}a_{k,\alpha}^{*}a_{k+q,\beta}$. The transverse rotation by $\theta$ about the generator is the mode rotation $U(\theta) = \exp(\theta J\sum_{k,\alpha}w_{\alpha}n_{k,\alpha})$ of synthesis.ladder-bosons-inherit-spin-statistics-from-the-single-modes (i), which acts by $a_{k,\alpha} \mapsto e^{-\theta w_{\alpha}J}a_{k,\alpha}$, with real weights $w_{\alpha}$, $W = \mathrm{diag}(w_{\alpha})$; the two chirality channels of a Dirac species have $w = \pm\tfrac12$ (Theorem \claimref{synthesis.light-ray-good-part-of-a-spinor-is-two-chirality-arrays}(iv)). $\rho_{q}(M)$ has helicity $h$ if the rotation multiplies it by $e^{h\theta J}$. The chiral sea $\Omega$ has every channel filled for $k < 0$ and empty for $k \ge 0$; a vector is edge-clean at depth $q$ if the lowest $q$ momenta are filled and the highest $q$ empty in every channel.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] \emph{(Window identity; the case $d = 1$, equal shifts, of synthesis.density-modes-bosonise-only-along-one-null-direction (i), the level-one $\mathfrak{u}(n)$ current algebra on a window.)} $[\rho_{q}(M), \rho_{q}(M')^{*}] = \sum_{k, k+q \in I}a_{k}^{*}MM'^{*}a_{k} - \sum_{k, k-q \in I}a_{k}^{*}M'^{*}Ma_{k}$ exactly, with $a_{k}^{*}Xa_{k} = \sum X_{\alpha\beta}a_{k,\alpha}^{*}a_{k,\beta}$; on edge-clean vectors it acts as $q\operatorname{tr}(M'^{*}M) + \rho_{0}([M, M'^{*}])$.
\item[(ii)] \emph{(Normality.)} For $N > q$, $[\rho_{q}(M), \rho_{q}(M')^{*}]$ is a scalar on the edge-clean vectors if and only if $[M, M'^{*}] = 0$; so $\rho_{q}(M)$ is a canonical boson there (value $q\operatorname{tr}(M^{*}M)$) if and only if $M$ is normal.
\item[(iii)] \emph{(Helicity.)} $\rho_{q}(M)$ has helicity $h$ if and only if $[W, M] = hM$. For $h \ne 0$ such an $M$ is nilpotent, hence, if nonzero, not normal: a pair mode of helicity $\pm1$ is never a canonical boson on the edge-clean vectors, its commutator there carrying the operator $\rho_{0}([M, M^{*}])$ (for $M = E_{+-}$ the difference of the channel numbers). If $\rho_{q}(M_{1}), \rho_{q}(M_{2})$ rotate as a vector ($J[W, M_{1}] = M_{2}$, $J[W, M_{2}] = -M_{1}$) and $[M_{i}, M_{j}^{*}] = 0$ for all $i, j$, then $M_{1} = M_{2} = 0$: no two pair modes with central mutual commutators form a rotation doublet. Normal helicity-zero modes (the channel densities among them) are canonical bosons.
\item[(iv)] \emph{(Quasi-spin.)} Let $M^{2} = 0$, $r = \operatorname{rank}M$, $N \ge q \ge 1$, $B = \rho_{q}(M)^{*}$. Then $|B^{p}\Omega|^{2} = (p!)^{2}e_{p}(x)$, $x$ the $qr$ numbers $\sigma_{s}^{2}$ (singular values of $M$, each repeated $q$ times), so $B^{p}\Omega = 0$ for $p > qr$ and $|B^{p}\Omega|^{2} < p!\,|B\Omega|^{2p}$ for $p \ge 2$. For $M = E_{+-}$: $|B^{p}\Omega|^{2} = (p!)^{2}\binom{q}{p}$ and $[\rho_{q}(M), B]B^{p}\Omega = (q - 2p)B^{p}\Omega$, the quasi-spin of $q$ sites.
\item[(v)] \emph{(Positivity.)} For every state $\omega$ of the tower and every $X$ with $\omega(X^{*}X) = 0$, $\omega([X, X^{*}]) = \omega(XX^{*}) \ge 0$. On the chiral sea every $\rho_{q}(M)$, $q \ge 1$, annihilates $\Omega$ and $\omega_{\Omega}([\rho_{q}(M), \rho_{q}(M)^{*}]) = q\operatorname{tr}(M^{*}M)$; on the reversed sea the value is $-q\operatorname{tr}(M^{*}M)$ and $\rho_{q}(M)^{*}$ annihilates. So, for the tower's positive adjoint, no pair mode of a tower state annihilates the state with a negative commutator, as the timelike polarisation of (K1) in Premise \claimref{synthesis.krein-form-premise-indefinite-inner-product-for-gauge-fields} would. The first sentence holds for every element $X$ of every algebra with a positive state; it is the reason Gupta and Bleuler need an indefinite form, not a property of pair modes. With a Krein adjoint $\eta X^{*}\eta$, $\eta$ a self-adjoint involution, a pair mode can be the timelike mode: on two modes with $\eta = 1 - 2n_{2}$, $X = a_{1}^{*}a_{2}$ and $\Omega$ the vector with mode $1$ filled and mode $2$ empty, $X\Omega = 0$, $\eta X^{*}\eta = -X^{*}$ and $[X, \eta X^{*}\eta]\Omega = -\Omega$.
\end{enumerate}
Clauses (i) to (v) are proved. \emph{Reading (argued).} On the window restriction of the null vacuum, the chiral sea (Theorem \claimref{synthesis.fluctuation-forms-of-the-tower-and-density-wave-bosons-of-the-null-vacuum}(vi)), the exact pair bosons are helicity-zero density waves; a helicity-one quantum about the generator built from pairs is a quasi-spin, of finite capacity $qr$, canonical only in the contraction over many two-level sites, with the channel-number difference as the obstruction operator; for transversally smeared flip modes over many generators that contraction is the mean-square statement of synthesis.null-plane-photon-data-and-the-pair-currents-of-the-generators (v). So the tower gives the photon's canonical relations from pairs at most as a contraction, and no pair mode is the timelike mode of (K1) for the tower's positive adjoint; with a Krein adjoint $\eta X^{*}\eta$ (as (KF) and \claimref{synthesis.self-adjoint-brst-charge-needs-a-krein-form-and-the-tower-supplies-the-ghosts} construct it) a pair mode can be, so (v) does not exclude (KF). The stored elementary photon (\claimref{field-theory.fock-space-maxwell-modes}) and (KF) are unchanged.

## technical
Take the modes on one null generator, labelled by a generator momentum $k$ in the window $I = \{-N, \dots, N - 1\}$ and a channel in a finite set, each a tower plane, with numbers in $\mathrm{span}\{1, J\}$ ($J$ the kernel bivector, commuting with every mode). Pair modes are $\rho_{q}(M) = \sum_{k}a_{k}^{*}Ma_{k+q}$ for a channel matrix $M$; the rotation about the generator multiplies channel $\alpha$ by $e^{-\theta w_{\alpha}J}$, with weights $\pm\tfrac12$ for the two chirality channels of a Dirac species. (i) Exactly, $[\rho_{q}(M), \rho_{q}(M')^{*}]$ is the sum of $a_{k}^{*}MM'^{*}a_{k}$ over $k$ with $k + q$ in the window minus the sum of $a_{k}^{*}M'^{*}Ma_{k}$ over $k$ with $k - q$ in the window; on vectors whose lowest $q$ momenta are filled and highest $q$ empty it is $q\operatorname{tr}(M'^{*}M) + \rho_{0}([M, M'^{*}])$. (ii) With a bulk momentum present, that is a scalar exactly when $[M, M'^{*}] = 0$, so $\rho_{q}(M)$ is a canonical boson exactly when $M$ is normal. (iii) Helicity $h$ means $[W, M] = hM$; for $h = \pm1$ the matrix is nilpotent and so, if nonzero, not normal: the commutator keeps the channel-number difference. Two linear polarisations rotating into each other cannot both be canonical with central mutual commutators, since $M_{1} \mp JM_{2}$ would be normal and nilpotent. Normal helicity-zero modes, such as the channel densities, are exact bosons. (iv) On the chiral sea a nilpotent mode of rank $r$ at momentum $q$ is a quasi-spin of $qr$ two-level sites: $|B^{p}\Omega|^{2} = (p!)^{2}e_{p}$, strictly below the Bose value for $p \ge 2$ and zero beyond $qr$ quanta; for the flip $E_{+-}$ the normalised commutator on $p$ quanta is $1 - 2p/q$. (v) A mode that annihilates a positive state has a nonnegative commutator in it, so for the positive adjoint no pair mode is the timelike Gupta-Bleuler mode that the Krein premise (KF) uses; this holds for every algebra with a positive state, and with a Krein adjoint $\eta X^{*}\eta$ a pair mode can be that mode, so (KF) is not excluded. Reading (argued): the null vacuum's exact pair bosons are helicity-zero density waves; helicity-one pair quanta exist only as the contraction of a quasi-spin over many sites (for smeared flip modes over many generators, the mean-square statement of synthesis.null-plane-photon-data-and-the-pair-currents-of-the-generators (v)); the elementary photon and (KF) stay as stored.

## lay
The graph already shows that ripples in the density of the fermions filling a light ray behave exactly like bosons. This result asks whether such ripples could be photons, which spin about their direction of motion (helicity one). On a single light ray the answer is no: the ripples that are exactly bosons do not spin, and the ripples that do spin behave like a finite collection of two-state switches, which fill up after a few quanta and only approach boson behaviour when very many of them are pooled. The indefinite bookkeeping that standard photon quantisation uses for its unphysical time-like polarisation also cannot come from these ripples with the fermions' own positive bookkeeping, because every state of the fermions has positive probabilities; an indefinite bookkeeping can still be imposed on them, as the standard construction does.

## one-liner
A fermion-pair mode on a null generator is a canonical boson on the window's edge-clean vectors iff its channel matrix is normal; helicity-one pair modes are nilpotent quasi-spins of q rank(M) sites, and for the tower's positive adjoint no pair mode is a Gupta-Bleuler timelike mode.

proofs.proof-main.tex:
\emph{Preliminaries.} The window identity (i) is the case $d = 1$ with equal shifts of the strip identity of synthesis.density-modes-bosonise-only-along-one-null-direction (i) (cited in plain text), the level-one $\mathfrak{u}(n)$ current algebra on a window; it is proved again here in the form used. The unit $J$ is the one justified by synthesis.kernel-bivector-is-the-unit-of-hermitian-boson-fields-on-the-tower, and the rotation in (iii) is the mode rotation of synthesis.ladder-bosons-inherit-spin-statistics-from-the-single-modes (i). By Theorem \claimref{tower.ladder-pairs-satisfy-car-vectors} the modes $a_{x}^{*} = v_{x}$, $a_{x} = w_{x}$ ($x = (k, \alpha)$) satisfy $\{a_{x}, a_{y}^{*}\} = \delta_{xy}$, $\{a_{x}, a_{y}\} = 0$, and $v_{x}^{*} = w_{x}$. $J = g_{1}g_{2}$ has $J^{2} = -g_{1}^{2}g_{2}^{2} = -1$ and $J^{*} = (-g_{2})(-g_{1}) = g_{2}g_{1} = -J$; every plane generator anticommutes with $g_{1}$ and with $g_{2}$ (Theorem \claimref{std-algebra.orthogonal-anticommute}), so $J$ commutes with every mode, and $\mathrm{span}\{1, J\}$ is a field ($\cong \C$, conjugation $J \mapsto -J$) commuting with the mode algebra. Channel vectors and matrices have entries in it, with the positive Hermitian form $\langle u, u'\rangle = \sum_{\alpha}\bar u_{\alpha}u'_{\alpha}$; for a channel vector $u$ the element $c_{k}(u) = \sum_{\alpha}\bar u_{\alpha}a_{k,\alpha}$ is a mode, and orthonormal $u$'s give modes obeying the same relations. For a matrix $A$ on the one-particle index set (momenta of $I$ times channels) write $\hat A = \sum_{x,y}A_{xy}a_{x}^{*}a_{y}$. From the relations, $[a_{x}^{*}a_{y}, a_{z}^{*}a_{u}] = \delta_{yz}a_{x}^{*}a_{u} - \delta_{ux}a_{z}^{*}a_{y}$, hence
\[
[\hat A, \hat B] = \widehat{[A, B]}, \qquad (\hat A)^{*} = \widehat{A^{*}} ,
\]
the second because $(c\,a_{x}^{*}a_{y})^{*} = \bar c\,a_{y}^{*}a_{x}$. Now $\rho_{q}(M) = \widehat{S_{q}\otimes M}$, where $S_{q}$ is the partial shift with $(S_{q})_{k,k+q} = 1$ for $k, k + q \in I$ and zero otherwise, and $\rho_{q}(M')^{*} = \widehat{S_{q}^{T}\otimes M'^{*}}$.

\emph{(i).} $[S_{q}\otimes M, S_{q}^{T}\otimes M'^{*}] = S_{q}S_{q}^{T}\otimes MM'^{*} - S_{q}^{T}S_{q}\otimes M'^{*}M$, and $S_{q}S_{q}^{T}$, $S_{q}^{T}S_{q}$ are the diagonal projections onto $\{k : k + q \in I\}$ and $\{k : k - q \in I\}$. This is the window identity. Write the first set as $I$ minus the top $q$ momenta and the second as $I$ minus the bottom $q$:
\[
[\rho_{q}(M), \rho_{q}(M')^{*}] = \rho_{0}([M, M'^{*}]) - \sum_{k\ \mathrm{top}}a_{k}^{*}MM'^{*}a_{k} + \sum_{k\ \mathrm{bottom}}a_{k}^{*}M'^{*}Ma_{k} .
\]
On an edge-clean vector every top mode is empty, so $a_{k,\beta}$ annihilates it for $k$ in the top $q$; every bottom mode is filled, so $a_{k,\alpha}^{*}a_{k,\beta}$ acts on it as $\delta_{\alpha\beta}$. The last sum therefore acts as $q\operatorname{tr}(M'^{*}M)$. For $M = M'$ and a single channel this is the edge identity of Theorem \claimref{hawking.current-commutator-exactly-edge-split}.

\emph{(ii).} If $[M, M'^{*}] = 0$ the value on edge-clean vectors is the scalar $q\operatorname{tr}(M'^{*}M)$. Conversely let $X = [M, M'^{*}] \ne 0$; $\operatorname{tr}X = 0$. Since $N > q$ there is a bulk momentum $k_{0}$ (neither top nor bottom). Let $\psi_{0}$ be the edge-clean vector in which every momentum other than $k_{0}$ is filled in every channel or empty in every channel, and $k_{0}$ is empty, and consider $c_{k_{0}}(u)^{*}\psi_{0}$, one particle at $k_{0}$ in the channel state $u$. At a filled momentum $a_{k}^{*}Xa_{k}$ acts as $\operatorname{tr}X = 0$, at an empty one as $0$, and at $k_{0}$ it maps $c_{k_{0}}(u)^{*}\psi_{0}$ to $c_{k_{0}}(Xu)^{*}\psi_{0}$. If $\rho_{0}(X)$ were a scalar on all edge-clean vectors, every $u$ would be an eigenvector of $X$ with one eigenvalue, so $X$ would be a multiple of the identity matrix, and $\operatorname{tr}X = 0$ makes it zero. So $[\rho_{q}(M), \rho_{q}(M')^{*}]$ is a scalar on the edge-clean vectors if and only if $[M, M'^{*}] = 0$; for $M = M'$, if and only if $M$ is normal.

\emph{(iii).} The rotation $a_{k,\alpha} \mapsto e^{-\theta w_{\alpha}J}a_{k,\alpha}$ preserves the relations (the factors are unit elements of $\mathrm{span}\{1, J\}$ commuting with the modes), and $(e^{-\theta w_{\alpha}J}a_{k,\alpha})^{*} = a_{k,\alpha}^{*}e^{\theta w_{\alpha}J}$, so $a_{k,\alpha}^{*}a_{k+q,\beta} \mapsto e^{\theta(w_{\alpha} - w_{\beta})J}a_{k,\alpha}^{*}a_{k+q,\beta}$ and $\rho_{q}(M) \mapsto \rho_{q}(e^{\theta JW}Me^{-\theta JW})$. This equals $e^{h\theta J}\rho_{q}(M)$ for every $\theta$ exactly when every nonzero entry has $w_{\alpha} - w_{\beta} = h$, that is $[W, M] = hM$. Then a nonzero entry of $M^{n}$ needs $w_{\alpha} - w_{\beta} = nh$, impossible once $n|h|$ exceeds the spread of the weights: $M$ is nilpotent. A normal nilpotent matrix is zero: normality gives $|Mx|^{2} = \langle x, M^{*}Mx\rangle = \langle x, MM^{*}x\rangle = |M^{*}x|^{2}$, so $\ker M = \ker M^{*} = (\operatorname{im}M)^{\perp}$; if $M^{2}x = 0$ then $Mx \in \ker M \cap \operatorname{im}M = 0$, so $\ker M^{2} = \ker M$, and by induction $\ker M^{n} = \ker M$, which is everything. Hence for $h \ne 0$ and $M \ne 0$, $[M, M^{*}] \ne 0$ and by (ii) $\rho_{q}(M)$ is not a canonical boson on the edge-clean vectors; its commutator there is $q\operatorname{tr}(M^{*}M) + \rho_{0}([M, M^{*}])$. For the two chirality channels of a Dirac species the weights are $\pm\tfrac12$ (Theorem \claimref{synthesis.light-ray-good-part-of-a-spinor-is-two-chirality-arrays}(iv)), so the helicity-one matrices are the multiples of $E_{+-}$ and the helicity-minus-one matrices those of $E_{-+}$; for $M = E_{+-}$, $[M, M^{*}] = E_{++} - E_{--}$ and $\rho_{0}([M, M^{*}])$ is the difference of the numbers in the two channels.
For the doublet, the rotation acts as $\rho_{q}(M_{1}) \mapsto \cos\theta\,\rho_{q}(M_{1}) + \sin\theta\,\rho_{q}(M_{2})$, $\rho_{q}(M_{2}) \mapsto -\sin\theta\,\rho_{q}(M_{1}) + \cos\theta\,\rho_{q}(M_{2})$ exactly when $J[W, M_{1}] = M_{2}$ and $J[W, M_{2}] = -M_{1}$ (differentiate at $\theta = 0$; conversely the linear system integrates to the rotation). Put $M_{\pm} = M_{1} \mp JM_{2}$. Then $J[W, M_{\pm}] = M_{2} \pm JM_{1} = \pm J M_{\pm}$, so $[W, M_{\pm}] = \pm M_{\pm}$, and $M_{\pm}$ is nilpotent. If $[M_{i}, M_{j}^{*}] = 0$ for $i, j \in \{1, 2\}$ then $[M_{\pm}, M_{\pm}^{*}] = [M_{1} \mp JM_{2}, M_{1}^{*} \pm JM_{2}^{*}]$ is a combination of the $[M_{i}, M_{j}^{*}]$ and vanishes, so $M_{\pm}$ is normal and nilpotent, hence zero, and $M_{1} = \tfrac12(M_{+} + M_{-}) = 0$, $M_{2} = \tfrac{J}{2}(M_{+} - M_{-}) = 0$.
A matrix with $[W, M] = 0$ that is normal gives, by (ii), the scalar $q\operatorname{tr}(M^{*}M)$ on edge-clean vectors; the channel densities $E_{\alpha\alpha}$ are such.

\emph{(iv).} Let $M^{2} = 0$, $r = \operatorname{rank}M$, and $N \ge q$. Write $M^{*} = \sum_{s=1}^{r}\sigma_{s}t_{s}u_{s}^{*}$ with $\sigma_{s} > 0$ and orthonormal families $(u_{s})$, $(t_{s})$ (the singular value decomposition over $\mathrm{span}\{1, J\}$); $M^{*2} = 0$ gives $\sigma_{s}\sigma_{r'}\langle u_{s}, t_{r'}\rangle = 0$, so every $u_{s}$ is orthogonal to every $t_{r'}$. Then $B = \rho_{q}(M)^{*} = \sum_{k}\sum_{s}\sigma_{s}\,c_{k+q}(t_{s})^{*}c_{k}(u_{s})$, the sum over $k, k + q \in I$. Apply $B$ repeatedly to $\Omega$. A term with $k + q < 0$ vanishes on every vector reached, since its target mode $c_{k+q}(t_{s})$ is filled: modes at negative momenta change only in the directions $u_{s'}$, which are orthogonal to every $t_{s}$; a term with $k \ge 0$ vanishes, since the only filled modes at momenta $\ge 0$ lie in the span of the $t$'s, orthogonal to $u_{s}$. The remaining terms have $k \in \{-q, \dots, -1\}$ and define $\sigma_{k,s}^{+} = c_{k+q}(t_{s})^{*}c_{k}(u_{s})$ on $qr$ distinct sites $(k, s)$: they commute pairwise (even elements of distinct modes) and square to zero, and the vectors $\prod_{(k,s)\in S}\sigma_{k,s}^{+}\Omega$ for distinct sets $S$ are orthonormal. Hence $B^{p}\Omega = p!\sum_{|S| = p}\prod_{(k,s)\in S}\sigma_{s}\sigma_{k,s}^{+}\Omega$ and
\[
|B^{p}\Omega|^{2} = (p!)^{2}e_{p}(x), \qquad x = (\sigma_{s}^{2})_{(k,s)}, \qquad |B\Omega|^{2} = e_{1}(x) = q\operatorname{tr}(M^{*}M),
\]
with $e_{p}$ the elementary symmetric polynomial: zero for $p > qr$. Expanding $e_{1}(x)^{p}$, the products with distinct indices give $p!\,e_{p}(x)$ and for $p \ge 2$ the products $x_{i}^{p} > 0$ are extra, so $|B^{p}\Omega|^{2} < p!\,|B\Omega|^{2p}$ for $p \ge 2$, whereas a canonical boson has equality. For $M = E_{+-}$, $r = 1$, $x = (1, \dots, 1)$ ($q$ entries), $|B^{p}\Omega|^{2} = (p!)^{2}\binom{q}{p}$. On the same vectors the terms of $\rho_{q}(M) = B^{*}$ outside the sites vanish by the same occupancy argument, and $[\sigma_{k}^{-}, \sigma_{k}^{+}] = 1 - 2\sigma_{k}^{+}\sigma_{k}^{-}$ on the two states of a site, so $[\rho_{q}(M), B]B^{p}\Omega = (q - 2p)B^{p}\Omega$: the normalised commutator is $1 - 2p/q$, the quasi-spin of $q$ sites of Proposition \claimref{field-theory.how-close-tower-comes-ccr} (there with $n$ pairs). For the same-channel density at $q = 1$, $D = \rho_{1}(E_{++})^{*}$, the moves $k \to k + 1$ chain, and $|D^{2}\Omega|^{2} = 2 = 2!\,|D\Omega|^{4}$ (computed on the window $N = 2$).

\emph{(v).} $\omega([X, X^{*}]) = \omega(XX^{*}) - \omega(X^{*}X) = \omega(XX^{*}) \ge 0$ when $\omega(X^{*}X) = 0$, by positivity of $\omega$. For $q \ge 1$, $\rho_{q}(M)\Omega = 0$: each term removes a particle at $k + q$ and adds one at $k < k + q$, impossible in the sea since $k + q < 0$ forces $k < 0$, filled. By (i) on the edge-clean vector $\Omega$ (here $N \ge q$), $\omega_{\Omega}([\rho_{q}(M), \rho_{q}(M)^{*}]) = q\operatorname{tr}(M^{*}M) + \omega_{\Omega}(\rho_{0}([M, M^{*}]))$, and $\omega_{\Omega}(\rho_{0}(X)) = N\operatorname{tr}X = 0$; the reversed sea (filled for $k \ge 0$) is edge-clean for the reflected window and gives $-q\operatorname{tr}(M^{*}M)$, with $\rho_{q}(M)^{*}$ annihilating it. The timelike mode of the Gupta-Bleuler form in (K1) of Premise \claimref{synthesis.krein-form-premise-indefinite-inner-product-for-gauge-fields} annihilates the vacuum and has $[a_{0}, a_{0}^{\dagger}] = -1$, which the first sentence excludes for every pair mode and every state of the tower, for the positive adjoint $*$. The first sentence uses only $\omega(Y^{*}Y) \ge 0$, so it holds for every element of every algebra with a positive state: it is why Gupta and Bleuler need an indefinite form. With a Krein adjoint $X^{\dagger} = \eta X^{*}\eta$ the conclusion fails for pair modes: on two modes take $\eta = 1 - 2n_{2}$ (self-adjoint, $\eta^{2} = 1$), $X = a_{1}^{*}a_{2}$ and $\Omega$ with mode $1$ filled and mode $2$ empty. Then $X\Omega = 0$; $\eta$ anticommutes with $a_{2}, a_{2}^{*}$ and commutes with $a_{1}, a_{1}^{*}$, so $X^{\dagger} = \eta a_{2}^{*}a_{1}\eta = -a_{2}^{*}a_{1} = -X^{*}$ and $[X, X^{\dagger}]\Omega = -[X, X^{*}]\Omega = -(n_{1} - n_{2})\Omega = -\Omega$. So (v) does not exclude Premise (KF), whose form is of this kind (as in \claimref{synthesis.self-adjoint-brst-charge-needs-a-krein-form-and-the-tower-supplies-the-ghosts}(ii)).

\emph{Checks.} The exact check verifies (i) on the window $N = 2$ with two channels for $q = 1, 2$ and nine pairs of six matrices (real and with $J$ entries, normal and nilpotent); (ii) at $q = 1$ on the edge-clean projector, including the values $q \pm 1$ of the helicity-one mode on two edge-clean states; (iii) the weights $\pm\tfrac12$, the doublet $M_{1} = E_{+-} + E_{-+}$, $M_{2} = J(E_{+-} - E_{-+})$ with $[M_{1}, M_{2}^{*}] \ne 0$, five integer helicity-one matrices on four channels, and the rotation at the half angle with $(\cos, \sin) = (\tfrac{12}{13}, \tfrac{5}{13})$; (iv) $q = 1, 2$, the Cartan comparison, a rank-one nilpotent rational $M$, and a rank-two helicity-one $M$ on four channels ($K = [[1, J], [0, 2]]$ in the block from the weight $-\tfrac12$ to the weight $+\tfrac12$ channels, $q = 1$: $|B^{p}\Omega|^{2} = 1, 6, 16, 0$); (v) $q = 1, 2$ on the sea and the reversed sea, and the Krein counter-model on two modes.
